# The DS3231 Module {.unnumbered}

The most common DS3231 clock module, sold under the name ZS-042, is a blue board of 38 × 22 mm with a holder for a coin cell on its back. It was designed for an Arduino powered at 5 V, with a rechargeable coin cell. On a station that runs on a battery for months, two of its parts matter. This appendix describes them, and the one change the [outdoor station](../Outdoor/00-design.qmd#the-clock) needs: removing the power LED.

## What is on the module

Besides the DS3231 itself, the board carries ([Arduino forum](https://forum.arduino.cc/t/zs-042-ds3231-rtc-module/268862/1), [hackaday.io](https://hackaday.io/project/164645/log/186609)):

- a **memory chip**, the AT24C32, at the I2C address 0x57: the station does not use it;
- a **power LED**, with its 1 kΩ resistor: it is lit as long as the module is powered;
- a **charging circuit** for the coin cell: a 200 Ω resistor (marked 201) and a diode, which bring the supply voltage to the cell;
- a **resistor network** of 4 × 4.7 kΩ: the pull-up resistors of the SCL, SDA, SQW and 32K lines.

## The power LED

The LED draws current all the time. On the module of a hackaday.io project, removing the resistor of the LED lowered the current of the whole module **from about 1.9 mA to 0.3–0.5 mA** ([hackaday.io](https://hackaday.io/project/164645/log/186609)). For comparison, the XIAO ESP32-S3 sleeps with 14 µA: with its LED, the clock module alone would draw more than everything else.

The LED, or its resistor, is removed. Either one is enough, since they are in series:

1. Find the LED: the smallest component of the board with two pads, next to the pins. When the module is powered, it is the one that lights.
2. Remove it with the tip of the soldering iron: heat one pad, then the other, and push the LED aside. Without a soldering iron, pushing it sideways with the tip of a small screwdriver also breaks it off its pads.
3. Power the module: no light any more. The clock works the same.

## The charging circuit

The circuit was made for a LIR2032, the rechargeable version of the coin cell. With a CR2032, which is not rechargeable, charging is a danger: a primary cell can leak, or swell. At 5 V, the circuit does charge the cell.

At 3.3 V, the supply of the station, the diode drops about 0.6 V: the cell sees about 2.7 V, less than its own 3 V, and no current flows into it. The circuit is then harmless, and stays as it is ([hackaday.io](https://hackaday.io/project/164645/log/186609)). If the module may one day be powered at 5 V with a CR2032, removing the 200 Ω resistor disables the charge.

## The pull-up resistors

The I2C bus and the alarm output (SQW) need pull-up resistors (see [Pull-Up and Pull-Down Resistors](01-pull-resistors.qmd)). The network of the module provides them: it stays.

Some projects cut it, or power the module only while they use it, to save its supply current. The station keeps the module powered all the time: the DS3231 then draws up to about 110 µA in standby, according to its [datasheet](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/DS3231.pdf). It is counted in the [energy of the outdoor station](../Outdoor/01-power.qmd#what-the-station-consumes).
